cim: Mesterséges intelligenciával teszteli a fizikai AI-t a Laplace
lead: A Laplace Intelligence AI-ügynököket és interaktív szimulációt használ az önvezető járművek és robotok biztonsági teszteléséhez.
osszefoglalo:
A Michigan-i Egyetemről indult [Laplace Intelligence](https://www.laplaceintelligence.com/) egy automatizált tesztelőrendszert fejlesztett ki a fizikai AI biztonsági elemzésére. A platform valós adatokból épít fel nagy pontosságú, interaktív szimulációs környezetet az Nvidia Cosmos alapjain, ahol az AI-ügynökök folyamatosan **ritka és veszélyes helyzeteket generálnak** az önvezető rendszerek és robotok számára.

A fejlesztők szöveges utasításokkal vagy valós idejű forgalmi adatokkal módosíthatják a szimulációt, a környezetben lévő szereplők pedig reagálnak egymás lépéseire. Az AI-ügynökök akár baleseti jelentésekből vagy hírekből is képesek automatikusan új teszthelyzeteket építeni, teljesen kiváltva a kézi forgatókönyv-tervezést.

A cég ügyfelei között van az Isuzu, a Bot Auto és az Nvidia is, amelyek elsősorban önvezető teherautók és okosváros-projektek tesztelésére használják a technológiát.
miert_szamit: A fizikai világba lépő AI-rendszereknél a szimulált biztonsági tesztelés kulcsfontosságúvá válik, mert **kiszűri a veszélyes szoftverhibákat** még az éles bevetés előtt.

If there’s one lesson the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident taught us, it’s that AI agents can be unpredictable.

“Imagine if something like that happened in the physical world,” Howie Sun, CEO and co-founder of Laplace Intelligence, told TechCrunch. “AI agents are moving from computers into the real world, and we don’t really want physical AI to fail in the real world.”

Ann Arbor-based Laplace is building automated red-teaming — essentially, stress-testing a system by deliberately trying to make it fail — for robotics and physical AI. The company is betting that the only way to make sure physical AI is safe is to have AI test it.

“Our goal is to help companies discover and fix problems before deployment—and, over time, build a shared foundation of evidence that customers, insurers, and regulators can trust,” Sun said.

Laplace is one of 20 startups competing in Startup Battlefield, TechCrunch Disrupt’s three-day pitch competition in downtown San Francisco. It will present on the Startup Battlefield stage Monday afternoon, October 13.

Sun, alongside his co-founder and chief scientist Henry Liu, founded Laplace a year ago out of the University of Michigan. Sun has spent the last eight years in academia researching how to challenge autonomous driving AI in simulation. In 2023, he and Liu — his then-PhD advisor — published a paper on the subject that made it onto the cover of the top scientific journal Nature. That’s when the calls started coming in from autonomous vehicle companies interested in implementing their ideas.

“I realized that I wanted to build this and take it from purely academic research into a product that’s useful in the real world,” Sun said.

Using their academic research as a base, Sun and Liu built Laplace, so named for “Laplace’s demon,” an 1814 thought experiment by French scholar Pierre-Simon Laplace that imagined that if you knew the exact state of everything in the universe, you could predict the future with total precision.

“We are essentially using simulation to predict the real world’s future,” Sun said.

At the startup’s core is a high-fidelity simulation reconstructed from the real world, paired with an AI agent that constantly probes for weaknesses and failure points. The goal is to ensure that any physical AI — be it a robot, autonomous vehicle, or smart city solution — is safe in simulation before it’s deployed in the real world.

The simulation environment is a post-trained version of Nvidia’s Cosmos, an AI world simulation platform, that’s grounded in the real world, allowing Laplace to reconstruct anything from an Arizona highway to a Paris pedestrian crossing. Simulations are generated by blending a mesh of different real-world information. A Google Street View image could serve as a reference from which an entire street is generated. But rather than generating something random, the simulator combines real-world map data to recreate an environment that’s true to scale.

Developers can then use language prompts to change the setting in real time, like adding in afternoon traffic. Sun says Laplace pulls real-time traffic and congestion information from navigation providers like TomTom.

Within Laplace’s simulations, not only the environment is simulated, but also the behavior of other actors. For example, during a demo, Sun directed the test agent vehicle to swerve into oncoming traffic. The car it would have hit — or driven through, as is common among some generative world models — moved out of its way to avoid a collision.

“It’s truly an interactive simulation environment,” Sun said. “Everyone is reacting to everything. …This is more like a world model with interactive participants.”
